Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 61
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: South Asian
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Paramedic
  trauma_type: Toxic chemical exposure
  pcl5: 35

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Workplace: Workplace, Darkness: Dark spaces, Olfactory (Alcohol): Alcohol smell
  Maladaptive Strategies: Rumination: Prevention: ruminate about how event could have been prevented, Constant Socialising: I keep myself constantly surrounded by people so I am never alone with my thoughts, Avoid Medical Cues: Hospitals/ Ambulances/ Physical Examinations
  Memory: Overwhelm on Recall: When the memory returns I feel so overwhelmed by emotion that I have to stop, Triggered Without Warning: Something in my surroundings can instantly bring back the full memory without warning, Terror on Recall: Remembering the event brings back the same terror I felt at the time

Vignette:
Rajesh, a sixty-one-year-old paramedic with decades of experience under his belt, remembered the night six months ago with crystalline, horrifying clarity. It was a call to an abandoned industrial site, a suspected chemical leak. The air, even before they reached the source, was thick with a sickly sweet, metallic tang that burned his nostrils, a scent he now associated with absolute terror. As they navigated the labyrinthine, unlit corridors by flashlight, the darkness pressed in, amplifying every creak and drip. Then came the unmistakable, sharp smell of cheap alcohol, mingling with the unknown chemicals, as they found the unconscious victim near a spilled drum and a broken bottle. Rajesh had felt a searing pain in his lungs, a desperate scramble for his respirator, and an overwhelming sense of helplessness as the caustic air filled his mouth.

Now, any hint of that specific chemical-alcohol blend, even a cleaning product in the ambulance bay or a passerby's breath, could instantly bring back the full memory without warning. Rajesh would be thrust back into the overwhelming sensory experience of that night, the terror on recall as potent as it was in the moment. The darkness of his own garage or the quiet, unlit corners of the paramedic station at night would trigger a similar surge of panic, his heart pounding, his breath catching. Even the familiar hum of the ambulance, once a source of comfort, now carried the faint, lingering scent of disinfectant that sometimes felt too close to the chemical tang, making the workplace itself a minefield of potential triggers. When these memories returned, he felt so overwhelmed by emotion, by the sheer force of the fear and the physical sensations, that he often had to stop whatever he was doing, needing several minutes to compose himself, his hands trembling.

Rajesh spent countless hours replaying the incident in his mind, dissecting every moment. He ruminated constantly about how the event could have been prevented, questioning if he could have donned his mask faster, if he should have waited for a hazmat team, or if there was anything he could have done differently to protect himself or the victim. He was certain that if he had just been more prepared, more cautious, the outcome might have been less terrifying. This relentless mental replay often robbed him of sleep, leaving him exhausted.

To combat the gnawing anxiety that accompanied these intrusive thoughts and memories, Rajesh had developed a new routine. He couldn't bear to be alone. After his shifts, he’d linger at the station, chatting with colleagues, or insist on going out for dinner with his wife, Sunita, and their grown children. He’d spend hours on the phone with his brother, or put on a podcast, anything to fill the silence in his home. He kept himself constantly surrounded by people, ensuring he was never alone with his thoughts. Sunita had noticed his increasing need for company, his restlessness when alone, and had gently expressed concern about his avoidance of quiet evenings together.

Perhaps the most challenging change was his relationship with his own health. Rajesh, a paramedic dedicated to others' well-being, now actively avoided medical cues related to himself. He would quickly drop off patients at the emergency room and retreat, avoiding the bustling corridors and the clinical smells of the hospital. He’d put off his annual physical examination, dismissing his wife’s worried questions about his persistent cough with vague assurances. He had come to believe that any thorough examination of his own body would only confirm a hidden damage, a ticking clock from that night, and the thought of receiving such news filled him with dread. He had been forced to take a few sick days recently due to overwhelming anxiety during a night shift, and it was Sunita’s persistent urging, coupled with his own fear of losing his ability to do the job he loved, that finally brought him to seek help. He desperately wanted to feel competent and at peace again, but what frightened him most was confronting the full scope of what that night had done to him.
